en.title: How much snow will Chamonix get next week? 27 cm up high, 23–29 November 2026
en.description: Chamonix's next week brings 27 cm at the top (8–46 cm range), peaking on Wednesday 25 November. Forecast for 23–29 November 2026.
en.lede: Next week's main event at Chamonix arrives on Wednesday 25 November, when 7 cm falls at the top (up to 11 cm in the best case). Over the full week of 23–29 November, the upper slopes around 2700 m will collect 27 cm in total, though the range runs wide: as little as 8 cm or as much as 46 cm.

sections.h: Snow depth by altitude across the week
p: The week breaks down into three bands. At the top around 2700 m you get 27 cm total (8–46 cm). Mid-mountain around 2000 m sees 25 cm (7–42 cm). The base near 1200 m receives 14 cm (2–25 cm).

Most of that falls on just four days: Tuesday 24 November brings 4 cm at the top (up to 9), Wednesday 25 gives 7 cm (up to 11), Thursday 26 adds 5 cm (up to 9), and Sunday 29 drops 5 cm (up to 8). The days between are nearly dry.

sections.h: Why the forecast range is so wide right now
p: One week out, storm tracks can still shift. The low of 8 cm and the high of 46 cm at the summit tell you the system could either brush past Chamonix or settle directly over it. That 38 cm spread is genuine uncertainty, not a flaw in the numbers.
Storm timing usually locks down first. The total—how much actually falls—tends to stay fluid until two or three days before. Watch for updates as Wednesday approaches.

sections.h: Where to ski for the freshest snow
p: Head to Les Grands Montets above Argentière. It is the highest lift-served terrain in the valley, and the north-facing upper bowls there are your best bet: they hold cold, unprocessed snow far longer than south-facing slopes do. By contrast, Brévent and Flégère sit across the valley facing south, so any new snow softens and bonds quickly as the sun works on it.

On Wednesday 25, the medium forecast is 7 cm at the top and 11 cm at the high end. That is enough to soften already-laid pistes but not deep enough for open powder. Use it to refresh lines that have been skied hard.

sections.h: The base gets some too, but watch for slush
p: The lower slopes around 1200 m pick up 14 cm for the week. That sounds reasonable, yet it is half what the top receives. Any mild spell will turn those low runs into heavy, sticky snow that drags on your skis.
The town and valley floor sit even lower and often stay wet when warmer air arrives. Plan to ski high and descend only when conditions suit you.

Before the first snowflake of this week falls, Chamonix should already hold strong reserves up high. From Tuesday 17 to Friday 20 November, the summit zones collect 92 cm (the range is 73–112 cm). The base, though, stays thin at 3 cm.
This coming storm arrives on top of that existing layer, adding depth rather than starting from bare ground. That matters for stability and skiability.

sections.h: How Chamonix stacks up against its neighbours
p: Courmayeur 18 km away forecasts 26 cm at the top; Flaine 20 km away gets 27 cm; Megève 25 km away also gets 27 cm. Chamonix itself: 27 cm at the top. Snow-wise, there is nothing between them.
The difference lies in terrain, aspect, altitude and crowds. If you are chasing fresh north-facing slopes, Chamonix's upper bowls stand out. If you prefer sunny runs, look south.

advice: Check the French avalanche forecast (BERA) for the Mont-Blanc massif before heading off-piste; fresh snow on a young base carries real risk.
Call the resort to confirm lift openings and operating dates; snow depth alone does not mean the cable cars are running.
Aim for Wednesday 25 November as your day: it carries the week's single best chance of soft new snow. Plan to ski high and early.
Pack layers for a wide swing: the summit can be 10–15°C colder than the base, and mild air in the valley may push the snow line up during the week.
If the high case of 46 cm materializes, adjust your lines upward and avoid the lower pistes; if you see only 8 cm, focus on north-facing terrain where old snow bonds well with fresh.
